title: 20 Investing Mistakes Beginners Make in 2027
description:
Investing has never been easier to start, and it's never been easier to make expensive beginner mistakes. In this video I go through 20 of them from three angles: the numbers (waiting, fees, skipping the match, taxes), the psychology (panic, hype, overconfidence) and the playbook (plans, simplicity, rebalancing), plus what to do instead of each one.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:34 How we got the numbers
1:59 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:07 1. Waiting to start
3:25 2. Ignoring fees
4:56 3. Skipping the employer match
5:59 4. Investing while carrying expensive debt
6:59 5. No emergency fund
7:57 6. Expecting the average every year
9:24 7. Ignoring taxes
10:40 Angle 2: The Psychology
10:57 8. Panic selling
12:17 9. Chasing last year's winners
13:35 10. Falling for hype
15:01 11. Overconfidence after early wins
15:54 12. Checking too often
17:09 13. Taking advice from social media
18:32 14. Too much in one company
19:49 Angle 3: The Playbook
20:01 15. No written plan
21:12 16. Too complicated
22:05 17. Using leverage and options too early
23:24 18. Never rebalancing
24:14 19. Forgetting old accounts and beneficiaries
25:32 20. Never increasing contributions
26:21 Why these mistakes are easier than ever
27:21 The beginner investor checklist
29:13 Mistakes by age
30:12 Two beginners
31:05 Questions people ask
32:49 Recap
33:24 What to do next

Sources:
- Investment Company Institute, Investment Company Fact Book: fund expense ratios
- Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit (credit card interest rates)
- S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA and Persistence Scorecards
- IRS, retirement accounts, contribution limits and capital gains tax rules
- SEC and FINRA investor alerts (pump and dump, finfluencers, leveraged ETFs, margin)
- Benartzi and Thaler, Myopic Loss Aversion and the Equity Premium Puzzle (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 1995)
- Barber and Odean, Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth (Journal of Finance, 2000)
- Thaler and Benartzi, Save More Tomorrow (Journal of Political Economy, 2004)
- Hendrik Bessembinder, Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills? (Journal of Financial Economics, 2018)
- Enron collapse (2001) and employee retirement losses, news and congressional record
- Growth examples: monthly compounding at stated average yearly returns (illustrations, not promises)
